Compliance · Zimbabwe

Hiring a drone survey in Zimbabwe: what the rules require

Drone operations in Zimbabwe are regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe (CAAZ) under the Civil Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft) Regulations, 2018, S.I. 271 of 2018. Every drone needs a CAAZ letter of approval and registration, and every pilot a remote pilot licence. Companies flying for commercial, corporate or non-profit purposes need an RPAS Operator Certificate with operations specifications, and commercial operators also need an Air Services Permit. CAAZ’s application adds security clearances and written approvals from landowners, local authorities and, where relevant, national parks. This page sets out the public rules and what to check before a drone team works on your wayleave, reserve or mining location.

As of 27 September 2026

This page summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice.

Request a proposal Checklist for clients

At a glance

Four approvals, then clearances and letters

The aircraft, the pilot and the operator are approved by CAAZ, and the commercial air service by the Ministry responsible for Transport. A commercial drone job also needs the security clearances and written approvals CAAZ’s application refers to.

CAAZ

Each aircraft

A letter of approval (s.4) and registration by CAAZ (s.5): “No remotely piloted aircraft shall be operated within Zimbabwe, unless it has been registered by the Authority.”

CAAZ

Each pilot

A remote pilot licence, valid for 2 years, with English at level 4 and a restricted radiotelephony certificate (ss.8–14).

CAAZ

The operator

An RPAS Operator Certificate (ROC) with operations specifications, valid for 1 year, for commercial, corporate and non-profit operations (ss.15–21).

Ministry responsible for Transport

The air service

An Air Services Permit for commercial operations (s.15(b)), applied for to the Ministry responsible for Transport (S.I. 69 of 2018, s.3(1)).

Around those approvals sits the site. CAAZ’s online application for organisations makes the applicant declare that it will obtain “all security clearances from Ministry of Defense, Ministry of Information Communication Technology and any other Agencies or Line Ministries as maybe appropriate”, and that it will fly only “after written Approval letters from land owners concerned, local authorities, national parks, state etc. in charge of the property/area of operation” (CAAZ online application). Along a pipeline or a line that crosses many farms, communal land and council areas, those letters and clearances all have to be in place; we found no published timetable for the clearances, so plan for them early.

S.I. 271 of 2018 is the current instrument: no later drone regulation appears on CAAZ’s legislation page or in the Veritas index of statutory instruments, as checked on 27 September 2026.

Regulators and approvals

Who approves what, layer by layer

Aviation safety is only one layer. Security, land, survey and data rules each add their own approvals.

Layer Body Instrument What it controls
Safety, aircraft, pilots, operators CAAZ Civil Aviation Act [Chapter 13:16]; S.I. 271 of 2018 Letter of approval, registration, remote pilot licence, ROC and operations specifications, operational approvals, frequency allocation (s.45(5)–(6))
Commercial permission Ministry responsible for Transport S.I. 271 s.15(b); S.I. 69 of 2018 s.3(1) Air Services Permit
Exemptions CAAZ Director-General S.I. 69 of 2023 Relief from specific rules, with a risk assessment and an “equivalent level of safety”
Security clearance Ministry of Defence, Ministry of ICT, “any other Agencies or Line Ministries” Declaration on CAAZ’s organisation form Clearance before operating; no public procedure was found
Import ZIMRA; Defence clearance at the port of entry S.I. 271 s.7; CAAZ FAQ Temporary import permit
Land and area Landowners, local authorities, national parks, the state CAAZ form; S.I. 271 ss.30 and 43 Written approval letters
Prohibited places The President; the courts Official Secrets Act ss.2, 3, 6 and 13 Defence works and declared places
Protected places and areas Minister of Home Affairs; police Protected Places and Areas Act ss.4–7 and 11 Entry, and directions that can restrict surveying, sketches and photographs
Aerial and space surveys Surveyor-General Land Survey Act s.7(1)(b) Supervision and control; no permit procedure was found
Personal data POTRAZ Cyber and Data Protection Act; S.I. 155 of 2024 Data controller licence, data protection officer, transfers abroad

The aircraft

Letter of approval, registration, and who may register

Letter of approval (s.4). It comes before registration. CAAZ decides within 30 days, the letter is valid for 12 months at first and then for 3 years, and applications must be in English.

Registration (s.5). CAAZ inspects the aircraft and will “vet” the owner or operator. It decides within 30 days; its FAQ says “most complete applications will be reviewed within one working week”. A change of ownership must be applied for within 30 days.

Who may register (s.6). A Zimbabwean citizen or permanent resident, or a body “whose principal place of business is in Zimbabwe”. A drone registered outside Zimbabwe, or owned by someone who is not eligible, cannot be registered.

Classes (First Schedule). Class 1 is below 2 kg and receives an approval letter; classes 2 to 7 run from 2 kg to larger than 150 kg and receive a certificate of registration. CAAZ’s FAQ says “all flying RPAs/drones should be registered”, and its 2025 annual report describes drones under 2 kg receiving letters of approval for custody.

What an organisation files

CAAZ’s online form asks a company for:

  • its representative’s Zimbabwe national ID or valid passport
  • the Certificate of Incorporation
  • the registered office notice
  • the list of directors and secretaries
  • a Tax Clearance Certificate
  • proof of drone ownership
  • a “Letter of resolution from the majority of the board (two thirds)”

“All documents must be provided in English.” The purposes offered include aerial survey.

The pilot

The remote pilot licence

Categories and ratings

Aeroplane, multi-rotor or hybrid VTOL, rated for VLOS, E-VLOS or B-VLOS flight. Pilots are 18 or over.

Medical, radio and English

A class 4 medical certificate for beyond-sight flight or aircraft of class 3 and above, a self-declared medical assessment otherwise; a restricted Certificate of Proficiency in Radiotelephony (Aeronautical); English at level 4.

Exam, training and test

A theory exam at an accredited centre within 90 days before the skills test, CAAZ-approved flight training, the skills test within 30 days of training, and the licence application within 30 days of the test.

The licence is valid for 2 years, with a revalidation check in the 90 days before it expires. It cannot be renewed once three years have passed since it expired, and logbooks are kept for 5 years (S.I. 271, ss.8–14).

The operator

The RPAS Operator Certificate and the Air Services Permit

The ROC (ss.15–21). Commercial, corporate and non-profit operations need an RPAS Operator Certificate with operations specifications. The application includes the certificate of registration and the letter of approval of each drone the certificate will cover, and the original operations manual for a first issue. A drone is registered under one ROC only; one ROC can list several drones, and it cannot be transferred. It is valid for 1 year, and renewal is applied for at least 60 days ahead. Extended line-of-sight work needs at least one trained observer aged 18 or over (s.21(2)).

The Air Services Permit (s.15(b)). Commercial operators also need an Air Services Permit, applied for to the Ministry responsible for Transport under S.I. 69 of 2018, s.3(1). Whether the aerial-work operator certificate in S.I. 69 of 2018 also applies to drones on top of the ROC is a question to put to CAAZ in writing.

Frequencies (s.45(5)–(6)). CAAZ allocates the frequencies the drone uses, on application.

What the operator must keep up

  • An approved operations manual (s.22) and records kept for 2 years (s.23)
  • A safety management system (s.24)
  • Security (s.25): background checks, criminal record checks every two years, security awareness training, secure storage and a security coordinator
  • CAAZ audits, which can extend to “partners, suppliers or subcontractors” (s.26)
  • Third-party insurance “at all times” (s.28)
  • An approved C2 datalink (s.36) and maintenance programme (s.56(2))
  • CAAZ approval for accessory equipment “not covered in the original design” (s.68), such as a new sensor payload

Security, land and restricted places

The clearances and letters around every flight

Security clearances and land approvals

CAAZ’s organisation form commits the applicant to obtain the security clearances of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of ICT and any other agency or line ministry that is appropriate, and to fly only with written approval letters from the landowners, local authorities, national parks and state bodies in charge of the area. No public procedure or timetable for the clearances was found. CAAZ’s FAQ says a “ZIMRA or Defense clearance” for an imported drone “may be obtained at the port of entry”.

For a corridor, that means letters from the owners and occupiers along the route, the rural district or urban councils, the parks authority where the route crosses a park, and the asset owner within 30 m of towers, pump stations and substations (s.43). Take-off or landing on a public road also needs the local authority (s.30).

Prohibited and protected places

  • Official Secrets Act [Chapter 11:09], s.3. For “any purpose prejudicial to the safety or interests of Zimbabwe”, it is an offence to approach, inspect, pass over or enter a prohibited place, or to obtain, record or publish information useful to an enemy, with up to 25 years’ imprisonment. Prohibited places include defence works, military and air force establishments and places the President declares by order (ss.2 and 13) (Veritas).
  • Protected Places and Areas Act [Chapter 11:12]. The Minister of Home Affairs may declare a protected place or area (ss.4–6). The order is served on the owner or occupier by a police officer (s.7) and is not published, and its directions may restrict “surveying or making sketches or taking photographs”. Whether those directions reach overflight or remote imaging is a question for counsel.
  • Key points (s.39(3)). Operations “adjacent to or above” a national key point or strategic installation need CAAZ approval. We found no public list of key points; the asset owner is the one to ask.

Operating rules

The Part V rules that shape a corridor flight

Only with CAAZ approval (s.39(3))

Above 400 ft; within 3 NM of an aerodrome; in restricted or prohibited airspace; adjacent to or above a nuclear power plant, prison, police station, crime scene, court, national key point or strategic installation. This is an approval route for an operator whose certificate covers it, not an outright ban.

Line of sight (ss.2, 40)

VLOS: below 400 ft and within 500 m. E-VLOS: below 400 ft, with an observer up to 1,000 m from the pilot. BVLOS only with CAAZ approval under the operator’s certificate, in visual conditions and below 400 ft unless approved.

People, structures, roads (ss.42–44)

Not over or within 30 m of people, unless it is an approved operation under the operator’s certificate, or the people are part of the operation and under the operator’s control; not within 30 m of a structure without an approved operation and the owner’s permission; not over, along or within 30 m of a public road without approval and safety measures.

Night (s.41)

Only reduced line of sight, or an operator whose certificate approves each drone for night flight. Night flight in controlled airspace needs a separate approval.

Aerodromes and radio (ss.31, 44, 45)

Never over an aerodrome or approach path without approval. Within 3 NM of an aerodrome the pilot carries an air-band radio unless flying reduced line of sight, and uses the registration as the call-sign.

Reports and defects (s.69)

Defects are notified to CAAZ within 24 hours for drones of 20 kg or more, and for lighter drones after serious incidents or accidents.

What this means for a pipeline or line. Plan legs of up to 500 m within sight, or up to 1,000 m with an observer; expect to need the asset owner’s letter near every tower, pump station and substation; and check the 3 NM aerodrome rule and the 30 m road rule at every crossing. Other rules: no towing, aerobatics or swarm flights without approval (s.39(2)), nothing dropped (s.32), no alcohol for 8 hours before duty (s.35), a first-aid kit and a fire extinguisher at the ground station (ss.53–54), and way given to manned aircraft (s.49).

Importing a drone

Temporary import, pre-clearance and the port of entry

S.I. 271 allows temporary import for “private, corporate, non-profit operations or commercial use” (s.7). It needs:

  • CAAZ pre-clearance at least 30 days before entry, giving the owner, country of registration, model, serial number, weight, specifications, purpose, period and place of operation; the pre-clearance is valid for 3 months;
  • a ZIMRA temporary import permit on entry;
  • at the border, the clearance CAAZ’s FAQ describes: ZIMRA or Defence clearance “may be obtained at the port of entry into the country and upon declaration that you would like to clear your RPA/drone”.

Sellers must tell buyers about CAAZ’s requirements (s.64), and maintenance technicians must be citizens, permanent residents or work-permit holders (s.58).

Temporary import is not an operator certificate

Temporary import under s.7 does not by itself register the drone, and an ROC application includes the certificate of registration of each drone it covers (s.16(2)(a)). Ask the operator which Zimbabwean registration and certificate each drone on your job flies under.

Survey and data

What the orthophoto is, and who holds the data

Survey law

The Land Survey Act [Chapter 20:12] reserves surveys for Deeds Registry diagrams and general plans, and boundary and beacon surveys, to practising land surveyors, and forbids anyone else to “hold himself out in any manner whatever as a land surveyor” (s.16). Section 7(1)(b) gives the Surveyor-General supervision and control of “all matters pertaining to aerial and space surveys conducted and geoinformation obtained in relation to Zimbabwe”; no registration, deposit or permit rule under it was found.

A drone orthophoto, and a structure register built from it, is a mapping record. Where your deliverable must be relied on as a survey, it needs a registered land surveyor’s certification.

Personal data

  • The authority. Under the Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07], POTRAZ is the Data Protection Authority (s.5). Structure registers linked to occupants, as in resettlement work, are personal information.
  • Licensing. S.I. 155 of 2024 requires a data controller licence, in tiers from 50 data subjects upwards, valid for 12 months, and a data protection officer.
  • Breaches. POTRAZ must be notified within 24 hours on form DP3, and data subjects within 72 hours when the risk is high.
  • Transfers abroad. POTRAZ is notified first, with a DPIA, express consent, adequacy and a data-sharing agreement (CDPG 5 of 2024). A controller not established in Zimbabwe that uses means located there designates a local representative (s.4(3)).
  • Processors. A processor works under a written contract with the controller (s.18(5)). Veritas reports POTRAZ inspections from 1 September 2026.

Penalties

Why the paperwork matters

Flying an unregistered drone
up to level 14 or 15 years (S.I. 271 s.5(11))
Breaking a Part V operating rule
up to level 14 or 2 years (s.55)
Commercial aerial work without the certificate
up to level 12 or 1 year (S.I. 69 of 2018 s.3(10))
Official Secrets Act s.3
up to 25 years
Protected Places and Areas Act
up to level 7 or 2 years
Holding out as a land surveyor
up to level 6 or 6 months (Land Survey Act s.16)

The Civil Aviation Amendment Act, 2024 also adds a civil-penalty order regime to the Civil Aviation Act. Processing personal information without a data controller licence carries up to level 11 or 7 years (Cyber and Data Protection Act; S.I. 155 of 2024).

For clients

Thirteen checks before a drone team works on your land

Ask for each item in writing, and keep copies with the contract.

  1. The operator certificate covers the flight

    The ROC and operations specifications cover what you plan: beyond-sight legs, night flight, work near structures, roads, aerodromes or key points.

  2. The Air Services Permit

    For commercial work, from the Ministry responsible for Transport.

  3. Each drone’s registration and letter of approval

    CAAZ registration and a current letter of approval for every aircraft on the job.

  4. Each pilot’s licence

    A remote pilot licence with the right category and ratings, and the radiotelephony certificate.

  5. Insurance

    Third-party insurance (s.28) and professional indemnity.

  6. Security clearances

    From the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of ICT, with a written plan for any key point on the route.

  7. Prohibited and protected places

    Whether any site on the route is a protected place or area, or a prohibited place. Ask the asset owner: the orders are served on owners, not published.

  8. Letters from the land

    From landowners, local authorities and the rural district council, national parks and the asset owner, including the owner’s permission within 30 m of a structure.

  9. Imported drones

    CAAZ pre-clearance and the ZIMRA temporary import permit.

  10. The operator’s security controls

    Vetting, criminal record checks and a security coordinator. Your organisation may be audited as a “partner” (s.26).

  11. Data terms

    Controller and processor roles, the POTRAZ licence where needed, the data protection officer, where the data are stored, transfers notified, and breach notice within 24 hours.

  12. No publication without approval

    No imagery of prohibited or protected places is published, and nothing is used for marketing without your written approval.

  13. A land surveyor where it must be a survey

    Certification by a registered land surveyor where the deliverable must be legally relied on as a survey.

How AfriScan works within these rules

Satellite first, drones where the approvals are in place

Satellite and your own imagery. A wayleave, pipeline-reserve or mining-location job starts from your route or boundary file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. No aircraft flies, so the aviation approvals above do not apply to that work, and it can cover a whole route without a letter from every landholder along it. Counsel has yet to confirm how the Land Survey Act s.7(1)(b), the Official Secrets Act and the Protected Places and Areas Act apply to satellite mapping (see the FAQ), and the data rules apply to any register linked to occupants, whatever the imagery.

Drone detail. Where a stretch needs more detail than satellite imagery shows, drone surveys are subject to the CAAZ approvals and the security clearances each operation requires. Afridrone is working towards the approvals Zimbabwe requires. Every drone proposal names the company that will fly and its CAAZ approvals, so your team can check them against the list above.

The imagery you already fly. CAAZ’s 2025 annual report records 54 drones over 2 kg registered that year. If your own team or a Zimbabwean contractor already flies your assets, send the orthophotos: we run the structure, change and corridor analysis on them, and a person reviews every result.

What we deliver from the air

  • Structure registers measured to your line or boundary
  • New and removed structures between dated images
  • Fresh excavations, pits and tracks, flagged for your teams to check
  • PDF reports and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Last reviewed: 27 September 2026. This page summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice. Drone surveys are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires. Satellite-based work involves no drone flight.

Frequently asked questions

Does a satellite corridor survey need CAAZ approval?

No aircraft flies, so S.I. 271 of 2018 does not apply to the satellite work itself, and no permit procedure for satellite analysis was found when this page was reviewed. Three points are open for Zimbabwean counsel. The Land Survey Act gives the Surveyor-General supervision and control of “all matters pertaining to aerial and space surveys conducted and geoinformation obtained in relation to Zimbabwe” (s.7(1)(b)), and no registration, deposit or permit rule under it was found. Counsel has yet to confirm how that section, the Official Secrets Act and the Protected Places and Areas Act apply to satellite mapping. Either way, imagery of prohibited or protected places is never published.

Can a foreign company register and fly a drone in Zimbabwe?

Registration is open only to Zimbabwean citizens, permanent residents and bodies whose principal place of business is in Zimbabwe, and a drone registered outside Zimbabwe cannot be registered (s.6). A drone can be imported temporarily for commercial use (s.7), but an RPAS Operator Certificate application includes the certificate of registration of each drone it covers (s.16(2)(a)). The regulations’ Second Schedule also lists a “Foreign Operator’s Permit” that no section of the regulations describes, so ask CAAZ in writing what it allows. Read together, the rules point to two routes: a Zimbabwe-registered company with its own approvals, or a Zimbabwean operator whose certificate covers the work.

How long does a remote pilot licence last?

Two years. The revalidation check falls in the 90 days before expiry, a licence cannot be renewed once three years have passed since it expired, and pilots keep their logbooks for 5 years (S.I. 271, ss.8–14).

Can a drone fly beyond the pilot's sight along a power line or pipeline?

Only for an operator whose RPAS Operator Certificate and operations specifications cover beyond-visual-line-of-sight flight, with CAAZ approval, in visual meteorological conditions and below 400 ft unless approved otherwise (s.40). Otherwise a corridor is flown in legs within the pilot’s sight up to 500 m away, or with a trained observer keeping visual contact up to 1,000 m from the pilot (s.2).

Do we need permission to fly near our own substation, pump station or depot?

A drone may not fly within 30 m of a structure or building unless it is an approved operation under the operator’s certificate and the owner has given permission (s.43), so your written permission is part of the file for your own assets. Operations “adjacent to or above” a national key point or strategic installation need CAAZ approval (s.39(3)); we found no public list of key points. Protected-place orders are served on the owner or occupier rather than published, so your security team is the one that knows whether a site has that status.

How long does CAAZ take to decide?

The regulations give CAAZ 30 days to decide a complete application for a letter of approval and for registration (ss.4–5), and CAAZ’s FAQ says most complete registration applications are reviewed within one working week. We found no published procedure or timetable for the security clearances CAAZ’s form refers to, so plan for them separately and early.

Can the drone orthophoto be used as a land survey?

Not on its own. Surveys for Deeds Registry diagrams and general plans, and boundary and beacon surveys, are reserved to practising land surveyors (Land Survey Act s.16). Where a deliverable must be relied on as a survey, it needs a registered land surveyor’s certification. Our registers and change reports are mapping records built from imagery; they show your surveyor and your wayleave officers where to look.

Start from satellite, and add drones where the approvals allow.

Send the route or boundary file and tell us which stretches or sites you want flown. We reply with a satellite scope, a drone plan that names the operator and the CAAZ approvals and clearances each flight needs, and a written proposal.
